intro: A clarinet and plucked cellos give the First Symphony a few minutes of ease. Even when the clarinet’s tune comes home, the middle section’s repeated notes keep dancing above it.

sections.label: A · Clarinet above plucked cellos
sections.mNote: The melody answers itself upside down

sections.label: B · Repeated notes in B major
sections.mNote: Wind notes alternate with descending string arpeggios in 6/8

cues.title: Clarinet and plucked cellos
cues.text: A clarinet wanders through a five-bar phrase above steadily plucked cellos. Its answer turns the same melody upside down: each rise becomes a fall. Bassoon and horn fill in the harmony, and the upper strings join near the end of the phrase.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 1, III, bars 1–10; Breitkopf & Härtel collected edition, IMSLP 317803. Phrase lengths and inversion: Kelly Dean Hansen, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Karlsruhe, 4 November 1876
cues.text: Otto Dessoff conducted the première in Karlsruhe on 4 November 1876. Brahms was forty-three. He had already called the symphony “long and not exactly amiable”, and audiences and critics split over it.
cues.evidence: Marc Mandel, Boston Symphony programme note: première in Karlsruhe under Otto Dessoff, Brahms’s age on finishing, his own verdict and the conflicting reactions. https://www.bso.org/works/symphony-no-1-in-c-minor . Brahms-Institut Lübeck work catalogue, Op. 68: https://brahmsinstitut.de/Archiv/web/bihl_digital/jb_werkekatalog/op_068.html

cues.title: F minor stirs the strings
cues.text: In F minor, the strings split a quick four-note pulse between high and low instruments. Clarinet begins an agitated melody; flute and oboe take it on. The easy walking pace has acquired a nervous accompaniment.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, III, bars 45–61; divided string pulsation and wind entries described in Hansen’s score guide. http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: B major, three against two
cues.text: The middle section steps into B major and 6/8. Winds repeat three notes; strings answer with falling broken chords. The beat now divides into threes, giving the exchange a buoyancy quite different from the clarinet’s opening stroll.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, III, bars 71–86; B-major trio in 6/8. Hansen, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Levi objects to the interlude
cues.text: Hermann Levi admires the finale, yet finds the two middle movements out of place in this great sweeping symphony. Here Brahms keeps the orchestra occupied with a clarinet tune, plucked strings and a brief dance in B major.
cues.evidence: Levi’s response to the First Symphony is reported by Marc Mandel, Boston Symphony programme note. https://www.bso.org/works/symphony-no-1-in-c-minor

cues.title: The clarinet has company
cues.text: The clarinet’s opening melody returns in A♭ major, with its plucked cello accompaniment. Above it, flutes and oboes keep playing the trio’s repeated notes as triplets. For a few bars, both sections sing at once.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, III, bars 115–125; clarinet reprise with the trio figure in upper winds. Hansen, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: A symphony for four hands
cues.text: In October 1877 the publisher Simrock issued the full score and, beside it, Brahms’s arrangement of the whole symphony for piano four hands. Two pianists could play all four movements, this clarinet tune included, at one keyboard.
cues.evidence: Brahms-Institut Lübeck work catalogue, Op. 68: first printing of the full score (Simrock, plate 7957) and of the arrangement for piano four hands (plate 7959), both October 1877: https://brahmsinstitut.de/Archiv/web/bihl_digital/jb_werkekatalog/op_068.html

cues.title: The trio says goodnight
cues.text: Poco a poco più tranquillo: gradually more tranquil. The trio’s repeated notes return softly in the violins, answered by falling broken chords in the lower strings. A brief turn through D♭ leads back to A♭; the final cadence waits for the winds and strings to finish their exchange.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, III, coda, bars 154–164; Hansen’s score guide. http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

transitions.title: E♭ becomes D♯
transitions.to: B · Repeated notes in B major
transitions.how: Clarinet, horn and violin descend through an E♭ chord while the cellos pluck upwards. E♭ becomes D♯, the third of B major. The metre changes from 2/4 to 6/8, and three repeated wind notes alternate with descending string arpeggios.
transitions.evidence: First Symphony, III, bars 62–78; Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.

transitions.title: Triplets cross into the old metre
transitions.from: B · Repeated notes in B major
transitions.how: D♯ turns back into E♭ as the strings hint at the opening tune in A♭ minor. The score returns to 2/4, but winds retain the trio’s repeated notes as triplets. A quiet plucked string descent prepares the clarinet’s return in A♭ major.
transitions.evidence: First Symphony, III, bars 109–114; Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.

transitions.title: The clarinet returns beneath the trio
transitions.to: A′ · Clarinet with the trio above
transitions.how: Plucked cellos recover their opening pulse in A♭ major. Clarinet and horn bring back the first phrase, while flutes and oboes continue the trio’s repeated-note triplets above it. The reprise is shorter than the opening section: its F-minor episode has gone.
transitions.evidence: First Symphony, III, bars 115–153; Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.

transitions.title: A cadence turns back to the trio
transitions.from: A′ · Clarinet with the trio above
transitions.to: Coda · The trio slows to a close
transitions.how: The approaching cadence opens into the trio’s repeated notes, now in violins, with descending arpeggios below. Brahms marks poco a poco più tranquillo. The strings turn briefly towards D♭; flutes, clarinets and bassoons answer gently and lead back to A♭.
transitions.evidence: First Symphony, III, bars 154–164; Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.

timeline.note: Clarinet melody above plucked cellos, with bassoon and horn harmony.
The opening tune passes to violins while clarinet adds a triplet counterline.
The tune turns to F minor above quick repeated notes in divided strings.
In the trio, repeated wind notes alternate with descending string broken chords.
The expanded trio gains trumpet support above active string arpeggios.
Strings anticipate the opening while winds retain the trio’s repeated-note pattern.
Clarinet returns to the opening melody while flute and oboe retain the trio’s triplets.
Quiet string and wind exchanges recall the trio’s pattern in the coda.

composer.epithet: He kept his First Symphony waiting until he was forty-three, then began the Second beside an Austrian lake the next summer.

composer.background:
In the autumn of 1853, a twenty-year-old pianist from Hamburg arrived at the Schumanns’ home in Düsseldorf with an introduction from Joseph Joachim. Johannes Brahms played his own music. Robert Schumann heard a composer of the future and announced him that October in an article called Neue Bahnen — New Paths. Publishers became interested. Brahms now had to live up to a public prophecy before most of the public had heard a note. The young man’s piano sonatas were enormous; the symphonies Schumann expected would take much longer.

Brahms’s father Johann Jakob earned his living playing instruments including the horn and double bass. His mother, Christiane Nissen, was a seamstress. Born in Hamburg in 1833, he studied piano with Otto Cossel and then piano and composition with Eduard Marxsen, who grounded him in Bach, Mozart and Beethoven. He played, arranged and accompanied for money. A tour with the Hungarian violinist Ede Reményi in 1853 brought him to Joachim, and Joachim sent him on to Düsseldorf.
